text: Chapter 3 covered the Glue Data Catalog as the shared metadata layer that makes S3 feel queryable. This lesson covers what sits one layer below that: the table format — the thing that decides whether updating one row means rewriting an entire partition, or a few kilobytes of metadata. A folder of plain Parquet files in S3 has no concept of a transaction, and no safe way for a reader to query it while a writer is mid-rewrite.

Iceberg tracks a table's state as an immutable sequence of snapshots — each one a complete, consistent list of exactly which data files make up the table at that moment. A write doesn't rewrite existing files; it writes new ones and atomically swaps in a new snapshot. That single idea unlocks row-level updates without touching a whole partition, safe concurrent reads and writes, schema evolution tracked as versioned metadata, and time travel — querying the table as it existed at a prior snapshot.

Amazon S3 Tables is a distinct S3 bucket type — a table bucket — purpose-built for storing data in Iceberg format, generally available since December 2024. You integrate a table bucket with your Glue Data Catalog directly from the S3 console, and once integrated, every Iceberg-aware query engine that already reads from the Glue Catalog can discover and query it the same way it queries any other registered table.

The real difference from managing your own Iceberg tables on a general-purpose bucket: S3 performs automatic maintenance on every table in a table bucket. Compaction, snapshot management, and unreferenced-file cleanup all happen without a separate Glue job or cron schedule to run and monitor yourself.

Nothing about how you write a SELECT statement changes. Athena queries S3 Tables with the same standard SQL this course already taught. Redshift Spectrum reads them the same way it reads other S3-backed external tables. And EMR Spark jobs can read and write Iceberg tables directly, for any pipeline doing heavier transformation than Athena or Glue ETL is suited for.

Apache Hudi is the other real table format with meaningful AWS support, but its footprint is narrower — no native Hudi support in Redshift Spectrum. For a new AWS-native lakehouse build today, Iceberg via S3 Tables is the broader-supported starting point. Next lesson: the permissions layer that sits on top of whatever table format you choose.
